puzzles.title: Rocks before the dragon
puzzles.premise: You are on the play. The opponent is at 7 life with an empty board and no cards in hand. Win by the end of your turn 2.
hints: Count the mana you will have on turn 2, and when each source has to come down to be ready.
Goldspan Dragon costs five. What else can you afford on turn 1, and what does your turn-1 mana pay for?
Look again at what Goldspan does when it attacks, and at which card in hand the Chrome Mox could swallow without hurting you.

lesson.rules: Mana rocks and Moxen are worth the most when they come down early: a permanent cast on turn 1 taps for mana on turn 2, while one cast on turn 2 only helps the spells after it. Chrome Mox exiles a card from your hand as it enters (imprint), so pick one you will not cast. Goldspan Dragon has haste, and its Treasure (which taps for two mana while Goldspan is in play) pays for a spell after combat.

puzzles.title: Dorks and colours
puzzles.premise: You are on the play. The opponent is at 4 life with an empty board and no cards in hand. Win by the end of your turn 3.
hints: Your Elves and Mystic make green mana. Which land lets you cast them, and which turn do they start working?
A creature you cast this turn cannot tap for mana this turn. Count how many mana sources you will have on turn 3.
Goldspan needs two red mana. Where does your red come from, and which land is therefore best kept for later?

lesson.rules: A creature cannot use a {T} ability (such as a mana ability) on the turn it comes under your control, so mana creatures want to be cast a turn early. Coloured costs must be paid with that colour: Llanowar Elves and Elvish Mystic only make green, so the first land has to be a Forest, and your red for Goldspan Dragon must come from Mountains.

puzzles.title: Feed the counterspell
puzzles.premise: You are on the play. The opponent is at 4 life with an empty board and holds cards you cannot see, one of them a piece of interaction. Win by the end of your turn 2.
hints: The opponent kept a blue card and an empty board. Free spells can be cast on turn 1 without any lands: what might they be?
A counterspell stops the first spell it is used on. Which of your spells can you afford to lose?
Your Ornithopter costs nothing and does nothing here. When would it be most useful to cast it?

lesson.rules: A counterspell answers one spell. If you cast a cheap, unimportant spell first, the opponent has to decide whether to spend the counter on it: an opponent who always counters the first spell it can (as the one in this puzzle does) wastes it on the bait. Force of Will can be cast for free by exiling another blue card from hand and paying 1 life, so it is live even when the opponent has no lands.

puzzles.title: Protect the dragon
puzzles.premise: You are on the play. The opponent is at 4 life with an empty board and a hand you cannot see: two lands to play, and one piece of interaction. Win by the end of your turn 3.
hints: The opponent is playing a land each turn. When will they have enough mana for a counterspell?
Count the mana you will have on turn 3. How much of it does the dragon use?
One card in your hand makes your spells uncounterable for the turn. When must it be cast for that to matter?

lesson.rules: Veil of Summer says spells you control cannot be countered this turn, but only from the moment it resolves. Cast it before the spell you want to protect. Playing the rocks (Sol Ring, Mind Stone) early left enough mana on turn 3 to cast both Veil of Summer and Goldspan Dragon.

puzzles.title: Two counters, two baits
puzzles.premise: You are on the play. The opponent is at 4 life with an empty board and five cards you cannot see. Win by the end of your turn 3.
hints: The opponent has five cards and will have lands. Think about which answers could exist at each point of the game, not only the first one.
Free answers work from turn 1; mana-based answers come online later. Do your baits need to be the same card?
You hold two spells that cost nothing, and the dragon is the only one that has to resolve.

lesson.rules: When the opponent has several answers, count them and make each one trade with something less important. A free counter like Force of Will is available from turn 1, while a Counterspell needs two untapped Islands, so the second bait is needed on turn 3 when their lands arrive. Keep the spells that do not matter for exactly this.

puzzles.title: Out of reach
puzzles.premise: You are on the play. The opponent is at 8 life with an empty board and a hand you cannot see: two lands and one piece of interaction. Win by the end of your turn 3.
hints: Eight damage with a four-power creature needs two attacks. What happens to a creature you leave alone at the end of your turn?
The opponent is keeping white mana open on your turn. Can you make your creature a bad target?
Lightning Greaves gives more than haste. Read both words.

lesson.rules: A creature with shroud cannot be the target of spells or abilities, so Swords to Plowshares has no legal target. Lightning Greaves gives haste and shroud and equips for {0}, which let Bloated Contaminator attack the turn it came down and survive the opponent's end-of-turn removal to attack again on turn 3.

puzzles.title: Through the deathtouch
puzzles.premise: Turn 10, your main phase. You are at 20 life; the opponent is at 8 with three untapped blockers and no cards in hand. Win this turn.
hints: Count the damage that gets through if every blocker takes one attacker each. Is it enough?
Look at what each of Kenrith's abilities does, and when it has to happen so that blockers cannot simply absorb the damage.
Wurmcoil Engine has deathtouch. How much damage does an attacker with deathtouch need to put on each blocker to kill it?

lesson.rules: A blocked creature without trample deals all its damage to the blockers. With trample, the attacker assigns lethal damage to each blocker and the rest to the player. Lethal damage for a deathtouch creature is just 1 per blocker, so Wurmcoil Engine with trample (from Kenrith) kills three chump blockers with 3 damage and tramples over for the other 3.

puzzles.title: Dragons in pairs
puzzles.premise: Turn 10, your main phase. You are at 12 life; the opponent is at 15 with one flying blocker and no cards in hand. Win this turn.

wrong.name: Pump instead of a second dragon

hints: Atarka alone is not enough. What in your hand can add damage this turn, and can it attack?
Read Atarka's ability: which creatures does it affect, and when?
A creature with double strike deals its damage twice. Which of your creatures would count?

lesson.rules: Atarka says whenever a Dragon you control attacks, it gains double strike until end of turn. Double strike means a creature deals combat damage twice (once in the first-strike step, once in the regular step), so Atarka deals 12 and a hasty Goldspan Dragon deals 8. Cast the haste Dragon before attacking so that it is attacking when the trigger happens.

puzzles.title: Pump the hydra
puzzles.premise: Turn 10, your main phase. You are at 12 life; the opponent is at 11 with a deathtouch blocker and two untapped Islands, and holds one card you cannot see. Win this turn.
hints: Work out how much damage the Hydra deals without help, and whether the blocker matters.
The opponent has two Islands open and one unseen card. What does a blue deck do with two open Islands?
You hold two spells. Does the order you cast them in matter?

lesson.rules: Kalonian Hydra doubles its +1/+1 counters when it attacks, and Berserk adds its power again and gives trample, so it tramples over the deathtouch blocker for lethal. The opponent's counterspell will answer the first spell it can, so lead with the spell you can afford to lose and keep Berserk for second.

puzzles.title: Clear the way
puzzles.premise: Turn 10, your main phase. You are at 12 life; the opponent is at 5 with one flying blocker, and holds two cards you cannot see, one of them a piece of interaction. Win this turn.
hints: The Dragon's damage is lethal if nothing blocks it. What can block it?
You have removal for the blocker. What could happen to a spell you cast on it?
You do not know what the opponent holds, but you hold two answers. What does a second answer do for you?

lesson.rules: Blockers are chosen after attackers, so a blocker has to be removed in the main phase before attacking. A creature with flying can only be blocked by a creature with flying or reach, which is why the Ornithopter matters. Holding two answers means a single counterspell cannot stop both: the first is countered, the second resolves.

puzzles.title: Count their counters
puzzles.mechanic: Baiting two counterspells with limited mana
puzzles.premise: Turn 10, your main phase. You are at 12 life; the opponent is at 11 with a deathtouch blocker and two untapped Islands, and holds four cards you cannot see. Win this turn.
hints: The opponent has four cards and two open Islands. How many of them could stop a spell right now?
You have four mana. Add up what your baits and your key spell cost.
Harmonize draws cards, but this turn the question is how few mana a bait can cost.

lesson.mechanic: Baiting two counterspells with limited mana
lesson.rules: Force of Will (free, by exiling a blue card and paying 1 life) and Counterspell (UU) each answer one spell, so two counters need two baits before the spell that matters. With only four mana, the baits have to be your cheapest spells: Blossoming Defense and Worldly Tutor cost one each, leaving one for Berserk.

puzzles.title: On the stack
puzzles.premise: Turn 10, your main phase. You are at 12 life; the opponent is at 11 with a deathtouch blocker and two untapped Plains, and holds four cards you cannot see. Win this turn.
hints: The Hydra is your whole turn. What are two open white mana for?
Spells resolve last in, first out. If the opponent answers your spell, can you answer their answer?
You hold two cards that make a creature untargetable. Do you need them before or after the opponent acts?

lesson.rules: Spells and abilities go on the stack and resolve last in, first out, and either player can respond while one is waiting. When the opponent targets the Hydra with Swords to Plowshares in response to Berserk, a spell that gives hexproof resolves first, so Swords has no legal target and does nothing. Protecting in advance, before the opponent has acted, only draws the removal at the protection spell and leaves you with nothing to respond with.
